meta.title: Nightbloom Soil Study 2024–2026 — readout
meta.description: Research readout of Nightbloom's two-year soil study on 48 jasmine and rose plots: regenerative farming stored far more soil carbon at a small, shrinking yield cost.

slides.eyebrow: Nightbloom Soil Study · 2024–2026 · Readout to the sourcing board
slides.heading: Regenerative flower farms stored nine times more soil carbon.
slides.lead: Two years, 48 plots, three growing regions. The yield cost was small and shrinking.
slides.notes: Give the answer in the first ten seconds. Every later slide is evidence or a caveat.

slides.heading: Three findings decide how we source jasmine and rose from 2027

cards.title: Carbon
cards.body: Regenerative plots gained 3.8 t of soil carbon per hectare; conventional plots gained 0.4 t.

cards.title: Yield
cards.body: Flower yield fell 11% in year one and only 3% in year two. Oil quality did not change.

cards.title: Practice
cards.body: Cover crops drove 41% of the carbon gain, more than compost or reduced tillage.

slides.heading: We claim regenerative sourcing, so we had to measure the soil
slides.body:
Situation: 212 farms supply our jasmine and rose.
Complication: our impact claims rested on supplier surveys, not soil.
slides.aside: Question: does regenerative farming store carbon, and what does it cost growers?

slides.heading: Method: paired plots, sampled every six months

stats.label: Plots: 8 regenerative and 8 conventional per region
Soil cores, 0–30 cm, Oct 2024 to Sep 2026

slides.heading: Pull a core from each plot and the carbon band is visible
slides.lead: Two cores from Isparta, September 2026. Amber marks carbon-rich soil.
slides.imageAlt: Two soil cores laid flat: the regenerative core is carbon-rich for the first 14 cm with roots; the conventional core for only 4 cm.

slides.heading: Regenerative plots gained 3.8 t of soil carbon per hectare, conventional 0.4 t
slides.lead: Change in soil organic carbon, 0–30 cm, Oct 2024 to Sep 2026. n = 48 plots, 1,152 cores. Source: Nightbloom Soil Study.

slides.quote: The first year I lost flowers and slept badly. This spring the soil held water through the heatwave, and my neighbours asked what I had changed.
slides.by: Kavitha Rajan, jasmine grower, Madurai, regenerative plot 14

slides.heading: The yield cost fell from 11% to 3% in year two
rows: Absolute oil per kg of flowers
Grower cost per kg of flowers

slides.heading: Cover crops drove 41% of the carbon gain, ahead of compost
slides.lead: Share of the regenerative carbon gain explained by each practice, mixed-effects model, n = 24 regenerative plots.

slides.heading: Cheap cover crops beat costly compost, and dry Isparta beat wet Grasse
slides.left:
Compost would drive most of the gain.
Rainy Grasse would store the most carbon.
Yield would fall 15% or more.
slides.right:
Cover crops drove 41%, compost 27%.
Isparta gained 3.7 t, Grasse 3.1 t.
Yield fell 11%, then 3%.

slides.heading: How far to trust it, and what to do
slides.lead: The caveats come before the recommendations.

slides.heading: Confidence is high for the direction and moderate for the size
We recommend cover crops first, because they give the most carbon per euro

items.label: Fund cover crops on all 212 supplier farms by 2028
Pay a 4% price premium through the year-one yield dip
Extend sampling to 60 cm and 5 years on 24 plots

slides.heading: Approve the €2.4M transition fund so every farm stores carbon by 2028
slides.lead: Approval today lets cover-crop seed reach growers before the March sowing window.
slides.notes: €1.3M + €0.8M + €0.3M = €2.4M. If asked about the limits, return to slide 12.
